The PAL color system has one significant advantage over NTSC - insensitivity to phase distortion. Multipath reflections can introduce such. The distortion shifts colors (eg purple skin, red tree leaves, etc.) This insensitivity means that PAL TVs don't need a Tint control.

Aside from the color system itself, nearly all PAL systems are used on 625 line/50 fps TVs. Most NTSC systems are used on 525 line/60 fps TVs. The spatial resolution of 625 line TV is better (sharper picture). However, the 50 fps results in more noticeable flicker (to my eyes, anyway).

ETA: it's all become academic, as HDTV and equivalents are sweeping away the old analog standards.

Slight phase variations that can occur over the air can cause minor (many people probably can't tell) color variations between transmitter and receiver. The PAL system uses analog memory (delay line) in the receiver and phase reversals in transmission to aid in cancelling this as the receiver compares the phase error between the current and previous lines and corrects them. I'm not sure if the errors occur when the signal is transmitted using frequency modulation (Wireless CCTV), but it does not occur on regular closed circuits.

This being said, unless you have a low power analog TV station in your area or live in a shithole country, these differences are now moot.
